items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: see the voice of the band was Marshall Royal, Snooky Young and Henry Coker, the lead players

ctx.x: It wasn’t as polished as the band in the late 50’s.

Right. We developed into a precision, a slick, precision, east coast jazz machine. But still, lots of feeling, the feeling never left. So the precision and the polish came, and the feeling, you know it just steamrolled over people. And with Joe Williams and Sonny Payne there too, and Marshall Royal playing lead alto, I mean he was, see the voice of the band was Marshall Royal, Snooky Young and Henry Coker, the lead players. And together they gave the band one hell-fired voice.
Yes they did. You’re making me cry for it.

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I had Benny Powell, Henry Coker and -- it wasn’t Al Grey.

ctx.x: He goes back to Ohio with you.

Right. I had the late Tate Houston on baritone. I had an old, straight-ahead, middle-of-the-road tenor saxophonist named Russ Andrews, who I think is now deceased, and for a while I had Roland Alexander playing tenor. I had Benny Powell, Henry Coker and -- it wasn’t Al Grey. Who was it playing trombone? Man, my memory fails me as far as the complete roster is concerned. I had Martin Banks, Virgil Jones, and Johnny Coles on trumpets. There were more whose names escape me. I don’t want to take up too much time…
Did you work with a certain constellation of musicians at that time, if I can call it that way, a certain circle of musicians that may be coming along?

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: Frank Wess and myself, Henry Coker and Benny Powell in an album called “No Count Basie,”

ctx.x: That was two tenor saxophones, two trombones. Frank Wess and myself, Henry Coker and Benny Powell in an album called “No Count Basie,” or Frank “East, North, South, Wess.”
Yeah but what was the date?
